children: MARKET WRAPS

STOCKS: Stocks finished mixed after strong jobs data and a muted rebound for AI companies failed to quell worries about the sustainability of the artificial-intelligence boom. Major indexes fell sharply for the week, with the S&P 500 registering its biggest loss since April 2025.
TREASURYS: Treasury yields rose after strong jobs data increased the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar rose sharply after the surprisingly strong jobs data.
COMMODITIES: Oil futures rose slightly, but finished the week with the largest losses in almost seven months.
HEADLINES
U.S. Adds a Hotter-Than-Expected 165K Jobs. The Fed Has Plenty of Room
for a Rate Hike.
The U.S. labor market crushed expectations in October, with
unemployment ticking down and employers adding far more jobs than
estimated. That will keep the Federal Reserve on track for an
interest-rate increase in December.
U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs to payrolls last month, the Bureau
of Labor Statistics reported Friday. That dramatically surpassed the
consensus forecast among economists surveyed by FactSet, which called for
a gain of 65,000 jobs following September's revised 60,000 payroll gain.
The national unemployment rate was 4.1% in October, ticking down from
September's 4.2% pace. It also marks 62 straight months of a jobless rate
that has remained under 5%. That's just shy of the record 64 months that
occurred from 1965 to 1970.
Tesla's Polarizing Cybertruck to Wind Down Production Amid Slow Sales
Tesla will wind down production of the Cybertruck at its gigafactory
in Texas next year, Chief Executive Elon Musk said.
In a post on X, Musk said the move is to "make room" for increased
production of its self-driving Cybercab-another proof point for Tesla's
thesis that its future lies in fully autonomous vehicles and robotics
rather than selling traditional cars.
The decision also comes as the stainless-steel pickup has suffered
from slow demand. In October, 1,914 Cybertrucks were registered in the
U.S., according to data from Motor Intelligence. By comparison, Ford sold
more than 70,000 F-Series trucks last month.
U.S. Consumer Mood Improved but Remained Gloomy This Month
Consumer sentiment logged an unexpected increase to begin November but
is still hovering not far above historically low levels, according to the
University of Michigan's monthly survey, a sign of the economic
discontent that powered Democrats' broad victories in this week's
elections.
The survey's preliminary November index reading landed at 51, in data
published Friday, compared with 48 in the final October reading.

Interviews for the preliminary reading took place Oct. 20 and Nov. 2,
so they wrapped up before results of Tuesday's election were known. A
final November reading, incorporating post-election interviews, will be
published later this month.
Moderna Swings to Profit, Lifts Outlook as Covid-19 Vaccine Demand
Stabilizes
Moderna returned to profitability in the recent quarter and lifted its
full-year revenue forecast, defying Wall Street expectations of continued
losses as international demand for its Covid-19 shots stabilized.
The biopharmaceutical company on Friday reported a third-quarter
profit of $162 million, compared with a loss of $200 million a year
earlier. Quarterly earnings came out to 38 cents a share. Analysts polled
by FactSet had expected a loss of $1.10 a share.
Total revenue jumped 29% to $1.31 billion, topping Wall Street
estimates for $890.3 million. The company attributed the gain in part to
higher Covid-19 vaccine sales in international markets.
Charter Continues to Lose Internet, Video Customers; Plans New Savings
Program
Charter Communications continued to lose internet and video
subscribers in the third quarter, dragging on its overall results.
The cable-and-broadband company also said it is rejiggering its
operating model for its core internet service to draw new customers and
better keep its existing customers, and announced a new cost-cutting plan
aimed at saving about $2 billion in annualized run-rate operating
expenses over the next year and a half.
The savings program will focus on eliminating what the company called
nonessential activities, as well as simplifying its organizational
structures and boosting efficiency through vendor partnerships.
Humana Lifts Outlook as Quarterly Revenue Jumps
Humana raised its full-year earnings outlook as consolidated income
and revenue rose in the recent quarter.
The health insurer said it now expects 2026 earnings of at least
$15.09 a share, up from a previous forecast of at least $6.52 a share. On
an adjusted basis, it lifted its full-year guidance to at least $9.50 a
share, up from at least $9 a share previously.
Analysts polled by FactSet are looking for earnings of $7.11 a share,
and for adjusted earnings of $9.16 a share.
Under Armour Revenue Falls on Broad Segment Declines
Under Armour posted lower revenue in its fiscal second quarter,
weighed down by a slump that cut across product categories and geographic
segments.
The sportswear brand said revenue fell 7% to $1.24 billion, compared
with Wall Street's expectations of $1.23 billion, based on FactSet.
Wholesale revenue decreased 6% to $725 million, while North American and
international revenue each decreased 7%.
Apparel revenue dropped 5% and footwear revenue was down 11%.
Outback Steakhouse Owner Raises Profit Outlook as Chain's Turnaround
Continues
Bloomin' Brands raised its full-year profit outlook and said its
Outback Steakhouse chain continues to make progress on its turnaround
plan.
The results came as the restaurant company, which also owns Carrabba's
Italian Grill and Bonefish Grill, posted a narrower third-quarter loss as
revenue gained, topping Wall Street's projection.
Bloomin' Brands said it now expects adjusted earnings per share of 97
cents to $1.02 for the year, up from its prior outlook of 90 cents to $1.
Brookfield Asset Management Fundraises $25 Billion in Quarter, Led by
Infrastructure Strategies
Brookfield Asset Management is seeing no let up in fundraising efforts
as it tracks toward a record year, driven by the alternative asset
manager's infrastructure franchise as investors seek out real assets for
stability and returns.
The New York firm said Friday it fundraised $25 billion in the
just-ended quarter, bringing the year-to-date total to $123 billion.
"Our fundraising is showing no signs of slowing down," Chief Executive
Connor Teskey said.
Norway's Oil Fund Reaches $224.5 Million Settlement With KPMG Over SVB
Collapse
Norway's oil-fund manager said it and a Swedish pension fund reached a
$224.5 million settlement in a class action against KPMG LLP arising from
the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank.
Norges Bank Investment Management, the arm of Norway's central bank
that manages the country's $2.3 trillion sovereign-wealth fund, said the
deal with the lender's former external auditor, KPMG, was reached on
behalf of investors.
KPMG said Friday that the settlement wasn't an admission of
wrongdoing.
Firefly Aerospace Inks $1.3 Billion Deal With AST SpaceMobile for Rocket
Engines
Firefly Aerospace reached an agreement worth more than $1.3 billion to
supply rocket engines and license its propulsion technology to AST
SpaceMobile, which is developing its own heavy-lift rocket.
Under the three-year agreement, Firefly will deliver 36 engines for
AST SpaceMobile's first three rockets, provide a license allowing AST to
manufacture the engines itself, and offer engineering support, the
companies said Friday.
Shares of Firefly Aerospace jumped 17%, to $17.80, in premarket trading. AST SpaceMobile's stock climbed 5.1%, to $31.75.

TALKING POINT Bank of America's Holly O'Neill: "I'm Very Bullish on What AI Has in Store for Us" As head of the retail bank at Bank of America, Holly O'Neill has her finger on the pulse of the U.S. consumer. Barron's spoke to her shortly after the bank's recent earnings announcement to learn about the financial health of consumers and hear highlights from the bank's results.

One of Barron's 100 Most Influential Women in U.S. Finance for the past five years, O'Neill also addressed how the bank is using AI, the financial advisor pipeline, and her own career as she celebrates her 30-year anniversary at the bank. An edited version of the conversation follows.

From your vantage point, how do you rate the financial health of U.S. consumers? We believe consumers are healthy. They are still spending, they have liquidity in their accounts from a credit perspective. We are seeing wage growth in lower-income cohorts and higher-income cohorts. Unemployment remains low. I think they are clearly in a good spot.

How did the recent quarter turn out? Are there highlights in your business? There were a few highlights for us as a consumer business. Our net income was $3.5 billion, up 2.4% year over year. That was off of revenue of $11.6 billion, which was up 4% year over year.

Within that, there were solid markers of organic growth. Deposits were up year-over-year for the sixth consecutive quarter. We saw net new checking growth of over 200,000 accounts and of those, the percentage of accounts considered primary is about 92%. We saw card growth up 5% year over year.

Another element was our BofA rewards program. We've seen over six million new enrollments since we launched in May, so that's exciting for us and will put us in a good position to continue to drive growth across the business. Across all of those markers, I think the business is very healthy.

Regulators recently fined Bank of America $1.2 billion for lapses related to money laundering rules. Does that change your outlook? Obviously financial crimes compliance is serious business. We take it seriously across the company and we're responsible for getting it right. The resolution is a step in the right direction. We're clear about the work that we've got to get done and I don't expect that it will distract us.
Amey Stone, Barron's
